Metagenomic and metatranscriptomic analyses implicated candidate genes associated with flavonoid transformation, with fcr and phy showing significantly higher transcript abundances in HTS than in CON and LTS. In vitro, tested Flavonifractor plautii and Eubacterium ramulus strains transformed selected flavonoids into phenolic acids with distinct substrate preferences under the conditions examined. Moreover, microbiota-associated metabolites, including hippuric acid, were detected in longissimus dorsi muscle. These findings characterize the spatiotemporal metabolic fate of sorghum (poly)phenols and support a role for gut microbiota in shaping their bioavailability and metabolic fate.

title: The microbiota-gut-testis axis: microbial metabolites as endocrine signals in testosterone regulation
abstract: From a microbial endocrinology perspective, this review evaluates three metabolite classes as candidate testosterone signals. None yet satisfies the three criteria required to establish a microbiota-mediated endocrine role in testosterone regulation—tissue exposure, receptor engagement, and biological effect. Herbal medicines show parallel improvements, but causal evidence is limited. A multi-omics functional validation roadmap is proposed to close these gaps.

title: Redox distribution of Asgard archaea and co-occurring taxa in microbial mats from an early Proterozoic ecosystem analog
abstract: Increasing evidence supports that eukaryotes originated from the symbiosis of an Asgard archaeon, the alphaproteobacterial ancestor of mitochondria, and possibly additional bacterial contributions. Eukaryogenesis likely occurred in redox-transition environments such as microbial mats or shallow sediments ~2 billion years ago, when atmospheric oxygen was far lower than today. We investigated Asgard-enriched microbial mats from the low-oxygen, sulfidic Catherine volcano lake (Afar region, Ethiopia), mimicking early Proterozoic conditions. 16S rRNA gene metabarcoding, metagenomics, and metagenome-assembled genome analyses across redox-stratified layers of in situ and mesocosm-maintained mats revealed that Asgardarchaeota thrived in the sulfate-reduction zone, mainly co-occurring with Desulfurobacterota-Myxococcota, among others. Lokiarchaeia and Thorarchaeia preferred anoxic layers. Within Heimdallarchaeia, Heimdallarchaeales were enriched in upper layers, correlating with oxygen-tolerant hydrogenase and sulfate-reduction genes, and Hodarchaeales, in anoxic layers, correlating with methanogenesis. Although reactive-oxygen-species defense mechanisms were widespread, Asgardarchaeota lacked aerobic respiration. These results support the hypothesis that Asgard archaea engaged primarily in syntrophic interactions with sulfate-reducers under early-Earth-like conditions.

title: Streptococcus alactolyticus confers colonization resistance against Salmonella by enhancing intestinal barrier integrity and moderating host inflammation in chicks
abstract: Salmonella Enteritidis poses a persistent threat to poultry production and public health. While gut microbiota (GM) is known to influence host resistance, the precise microbial and host genetic factors that confer protection remain poorly defined. This study aims to systematically dissect the interaction mechanisms among host genetic variations, specific gut microbes, and immunomodulatory metabolites, elucidating the genetic basis by which they jointly drive colonization resistance against Salmonella in chicks. Using a controlled infection model in chickens, we established a phenotypic colonization resistance (CR) index and identified distinct resistant and susceptible cohorts. Resistant chicks exhibited higher abundances of Streptococcus alactolyticus ( S. alactolyticus ). Dietary supplementation with S. alactolyticus reduced Salmonella load and enhanced intestinal mucosal integrity in challenged birds. Transcriptomic and serum metabolomic analyses ( S. alactolyticus vs PBS) showed that at 6 h post- Salmonella infection, differentially expressed genes were significantly enriched in the TGF-β signaling pathway, while differential metabolites were mainly enriched in energy metabolism pathways such as the TCA cycle. A genome-wide association study (GWAS) identified a locus on chromosome 2 that was significantly associated with S. alactolyticus abundance. Integrated with transcriptomic analysis, PDK4 was pinpointed as the leading candidate gene. This study describes the host genetic, metabolic regulatory, and gut microbiota factors that control Salmonella resistance in chickens, in which PDK4 may influence Salmonella colonization through modulation of S. alactolyticus . Our findings highlight novel pathways for enhancing disease resistance through targeted manipulation of gut microbiota and host genetics.

title: Uncovering lung virome signatures of COPD severity and acute exacerbations in longitudinally sampled AERIS cohort
authors: On behalf of the AERIS Study Group
abstract: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) is increasingly recognized as a complex disorder in which microbial communities may modulate disease progression and exacerbation risk. We investigated the contribution of the respiratory virome to disease severity and acute exacerbations in COPD using a comprehensive longitudinal dataset that simultaneously profiled eukaryotic viruses and bacteriophages across deeply phenotyped COPD subtypes. Sputum samples were collected longitudinally from 98 patients with a history of frequent exacerbations at the University Hospital Southampton between 2011 and 2013 as part of an observational cohort study. To characterize the lung virome in these patients, we analyzed 520 samples using high-throughput metagenomic sequencing. Viral genomes were identified in 424 of these samples with state-of-the-art bioinformatic methods. Ubiquitous anelloviruses exhibited a significant increase in their genus diversity with exacerbation events. Rhinoviruses were confirmed as primary viral triggers of flare-ups. Bacteriophage richness declined with increasing COPD severity, characterized by continuous impaired lung capacity and elevated airway obstruction. In addition, we detected Haemophilus -infecting phages carrying virulence factors or anti-phage defense systems in lungs with increased Haemophilus bacterial loads, suggesting that these phages are associated with bacterial fitness and microbial dysbiosis. We further demonstrated high inter-individual variability in virome composition, with exacerbation events consistently associated with more pronounced dysbiosis. Despite inherent challenges of sputum-based virome profiling, we performed, to our knowledge, the first longitudinal characterization of the COPD virome and reported underlying stability trends. Our findings emphasize that a deeper understanding of respiratory virome dynamics holds promise for identifying novel COPD biomarkers and developing targeted therapeutic strategies.

title: Gut microbiome features in methamphetamine use disorder: external validation of a candidate marker panel and exploratory multi-omics associations
abstract: Methamphetamine use disorder (MUD) is a chronic, relapsing disorder with symptoms most pronounced during withdrawal, yet objective biomarkers remain lacking. Although gut microbial alterations have been reported in substance use disorders, their potential as candidate markers, longitudinal patterns, and symptom associations in MUD remain unclear. Gut microbiota profiles were analysed in 103 participants with MUD and 80 healthy controls. Longitudinal analyses included 52 participants with MUD assessed at baseline and after 1, 3, and 6 months of withdrawal. Paired microbiome-metabolome profiling was performed in 29 participants with MUD at baseline and 1 month and in 29 matched healthy controls. A 30-taxon candidate microbial marker panel distinguished MUD from controls, achieving an external validation AUC of 0.821 (95% CI, 0.653-0.990). PERMANOVA detected no significant overall compositional change in the candidate marker panel across the withdrawal time points. Individual marker taxa nevertheless followed four distinct temporal trajectories. Exploratory multi-omics analyses identified associations between Ruminococcus gnavus and depressive symptoms, and between microbial L-arginine biosynthesis and sleep disturbance during early withdrawal. Plasma dopamine and caffeine were associated with components of these microbe-symptom relationships. This study identifies a candidate gut microbial marker panel for MUD and provides hypothesis-generating multi-omics insights into withdrawal-related symptoms.

title: Biofilm matrix-mediated localization potentiates antimicrobial activity in cariogenic biofilms
abstract: The extracellular polymeric substance (EPS) matrix serves as a structural scaffold for biofilm organization, contributing to structural integrity and antimicrobial tolerance by modulating the penetration and distribution of antimicrobial agents. However, whether this EPS matrix can also potentiate antimicrobial localization and activity remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated the role of the EPS matrix in erythrosine B (EB)-mediated killing of Streptococcus mutans within mature biofilms following brief topical exposure. Biofilms formed on saliva-coated hydroxyapatite discs were exposed to EB and evaluated for bactericidal activity, glycolytic acid production, and EB spatial distribution. EB markedly reduced viable bacteria in mature biofilms and suppressed glycolytic acid production. Confocal imaging revealed preferential localization of EB within EPS-rich regions of intact biofilms, whereas selective enzymatic disruption of the glucan-rich matrix, particularly following glucanohydrolases treatment, markedly reduced EB retention. Consistently, EB-mediated bactericidal activity was attenuated in biofilms grown under glucan-deficient conditions, in which sucrose-dependent glucan-rich matrix formation was limited. Together, these findings support a matrix-dependent antimicrobial model in which glucan-rich biofilm matrix promotes EB localization and retention, thereby enhancing bactericidal activity in mature biofilms. This work challenges the conventional view of the biofilm matrix solely as a protective barrier and highlights its broader role as a functional determinant of antimicrobial performance in mature biofilms.

title: Stachyose ameliorates polycystic ovary syndrome through the gut–BAT axis by promoting Alistipes sp. proliferation
abstract: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is associated with dysbiosis of the gut microbiota. Stachyose protects against various diseases caused by gut microbiota disturbances. We previously demonstrated that stachyose reduced testosterone levels and ameliorated estrous cycle disruption in PCOS rats. However, the mechanism was unclear. Here, stachyose treatment ameliorated ovarian dysfunction and insulin resistance (IR) in PCOS rats. Furthermore, stachyose promoted lipolysis in brown adipose tissue (BAT), which in turn enhanced BAT thermogenesis by indirectly upregulating thermogenic markers. 16S rDNA sequencing showed that stachyose significantly increased Alistipes sp . ( A.sp .) abundance in PCOS rats. In vitro, compared with lactose-treated group, stachyose promoted A.sp . proliferation in a time-dependent manner. Furthermore, oral gavage of A.sp . decreased serum testosterone, fasting glucose levels, body weight, and reshaped gut microbiota communities by increasing the abundance of beneficial microbes in PCOS rats. Importantly, A.sp . treatment increased ATGL, PGC-1α and UCP1 expression in the BAT of PCOS rats. This Suggest that stachyose ameliorates reproductive and metabolic disorders in PCOS through the gut-BAT axis: stachyose increases A.sp . abundance, triggering BAT lipolysis and driving UCP1-dependent thermogenesis and energy expenditure, ultimately mitigates both ovarian dysfunction and metabolic abnormalities. Collectively, these findings suggest that stachyose or A.sp . administration shows promise as a PCOS therapy.

title: The biofilm matrix of uropathogenic Escherichia coli contributes to antimicrobial resistance by reducing molecular transport
abstract: Biofilms are complex communities of microorganisms encased in an extracellular matrix (ECM) containing biomolecules such as proteins, extracellular DNA, polysaccharides and lipids. Here we investigated biofilms formed by uropathogenic Escherichia coli (UPEC), the major cause of urinary tract infections (UTIs), to understand how ECM comprised of curli amyloid fibres and the polysaccharide cellulose contributes to antimicrobial resistance. We used single-plane illumination microscopy combined with fluorescence correlation spectroscopy (SPIM-FCS) to quantify the diffusion of different sized molecules in UPEC biofilms. This approach generated high-resolution three-dimensional diffusion coefficient maps, demonstrating that biofilms containing curli fibres, with or without cellulose, exhibit reduced and spatially heterogeneous diffusion consistent with a molecular sieving effect that limits the transport of larger molecules through the ECM. In contrast, cellulose alone had little measurable impact on diffusion. We further demonstrate these UPEC biofilms exhibit resistance to the antimicrobial peptides LL-37 and polymyxin B, in part mediated by charge-dependent reduced diffusion. This behaviour is consistent with charge-mediated interactions with the biofilm ECM that reduce antimicrobial peptide penetration and thus promote the survival of biofilm-encased cells. The combined effect of charge-based interactions and molecular sieving leads to a significantly different distribution and mobility of differently charged peptides, providing a mechanism to explain reduced activity of cationic antimicrobial peptides in curli-positive biofilms.

title: G-quadruplex aptamer conjugate for the enhanced recognition and eradication of Staphylococcus aureus biofilms
abstract: Bacterial biofilm-associated infections remain a major challenge in clinical settings. Innovative solutions are therefore urgently needed to improve the efficacy of antibacterial agents and to overcome biofilm tolerance. In this study, we sought to enhance the selectivity of cytotoxic small molecules via conjugation with aptamers. We developed and characterized a biofilm-specific G-quadruplex aptamer hybrid loaded with 13-(4-ethenylbenzyl)berberine iodide, which exhibited potent antibiofilm activity against Staphylococcus aureus NCTC 8325-4. The incorporation of the G-quadruplex motif into the SA31 aptamer significantly improved biofilm binding and penetration. This work presents evidence of the interaction between G-quadruplex and Staphylococcal protein A, revealing biofilm targeting properties of this motif. Mechanistic investigations revealed that treatment of the tested strain with 13-(4-ethenylbenzyl)berberine iodide was associated with transcriptional changes in pathways related to DNA replication, cell wall biosynthesis, biofilm formation and quorum sensing. Collectively, our study highlights the potential of G-quadruplex aptamer hybrids as promising delivery platform for addressing the challenges posed by biofilm-associated infections.

title: Nonlocal interactions through hydrodynamics drive biofilm development and microbial competition in porous media
abstract: Microorganisms predominantly exist within soil-like environments as sessile communities called biofilms, where fluid dynamics critically shape their development and dispersal. Despite their central role in diverse systems, from biogeochemical processes to industrial filtration, oil recovery, groundwater contamination, and carbon sequestration, the mechanisms underlying biofilm-flow interactions in porous media remain poorly understood. Here, we combine microfluidic experiments with mathematical modeling to demonstrate that nonlocal interactions through hydrodynamic effects mediate intricate spatiotemporal dynamics and drive exploitative competition within porous media. Our results show that biofilms self-organize into clusters of biologically clogged channels interspersed with preferential flow paths (PFPs). PFP formation and stability result from feedbacks between local changes in hydraulic conductivity and global reorganization of flow patterns and pressure distribution. We reveal that PFPs tend to be unstable, with detachment of biofilm triggered when pressure differentials exceed critical thresholds. Based on simulations of competing populations, we suggest that these large-scale detachment events could be interpreted as an evolutionary trade-off, whereby bacterial matrices are sufficiently robust to withstand continuous shear stress while remaining sensitive to pressure-induced failure, thereby enabling nutrient access and avoiding redirection of resources toward competitors. The nonlocal nature of these hydrodynamic interactions shows that fitness in porous media must be thought of as a multiscale concept and provides new insights into bacterial adaptation strategies in porous environments. These findings further suggest targeted approaches for biofilm control in both natural and engineered systems.

title: A validation framework for translating ethnomicrobiology into microbiome-enabled desert restoration
abstract: Microbiome-based dryland restoration is promising but weakly validated. We develop ethnomicrobiology, the study of how human communities manage microbial processes, as a discovery-and-validation framework. A structured evidence map of 42 systems shows food fermentation is most mature, whereas restoration practices lag. We propose a five-level evidence-maturity ladder, from traditional observation to governed field deployment, and apply it to waste-biomass valorization, converting traditional practices into mechanistically tested, ethically governed restoration interventions.

title: Lactobacillus agilis in the small intestine reduce abdominal fat deposition in broilers by regulating lipid metabolism
abstract: Excessive fat deposition in broilers not only affects the taste and texture of the meat but also reduces feed conversion efficiency and increases breeding costs. Research has indicated that intestinal microorganisms play a crucial role in regulating lipid metabolism and enhancing meat quality. This study found that fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) from high-weight and low-abdominal-fat chickens to broilers significantly reduced fat deposition and downregulated hepatic lipid synthesis genes (LPL, ACSL1, FADS1) while upregulating catabolism genes (PPARα, HSL) ( P < 0.05). 16S rRNA analysis showed FMT increased beneficial jejunal bacteria like Lactobacillus . Subsequently, a strain of Lactobacillus agilis CIM-3 was isolated from the intestines of high-weight and low-abdominal-fat recipient chickens. Feeding trials confirmed CIM-3 reduces abdominal fat and improves growth performance. It increased cecal populations of SCFA-producing bacteria and elevated serum SCFA levels, while significantly decreased systemic and intestinal inflammatory markers (LPS, IL-1β, IL-8, TNF-α) ( P < 0.05). Mechanistically, CIM-3 upregulated hepatic P-AMPK and HSL and downregulated FAS and LPL ( P < 0.05). In conclusion, gut microbiota, particularly L. agilis CIM-3, plays a key role in regulating broiler lipid metabolism. The strain activates the AMPK signaling pathway by enhancing SCFA production and alleviating inflammation, leading to reduced lipid synthesis and fat deposition.

title: Environmental cues shape mucosal enteric glia networks independent of lamina propria innervation
abstract: Mucosal enteric glia are implicated in different aspects of gut function but the determinants of their occupancy of the lamina propria remain obscure. Analyzing mucosal enteric glia during intestinal inflammation and in mouse models differing for diet and gut microbiota, we found that colitis drastically impacts glial network organization, and that diet modulates mucosal glia cyto-architecture, with microbiota inducing intestinal region-specific variations. Restored by conventionalization, germ-free mice exhibit reduced mucosal glia numbers throughout the intestine. Vagotomy affects mucosal enteric glia maintenance in a diet-dependent fashion but does not influence lamina propria colonization. Also, differences in nerve fiber density fail to account for the variations in mucosal enteric glia networks. Providing insight into their interaction with neuronal components and the luminal milieu, our results emphasize the profound plasticity of enteric glia, and suggest that their presence in the mucosa is not merely configured by lamina propria innervation.

title: Recovering anaerobic bacterial genomes in saliva, tumour and blood whole genome sequencing data from patients with prostate cancer
abstract: Microbial constituents in the gastrointestinal tract, the urine and prostate tissue are being linked with clinical differences in prostate cancer, and a recent meta-analysis has linked periodontal disease to this cancer. Several hypotheses exist regarding how specific bacteria can contribute towards the development of prostate cancer. Recovering microbial genomes, and their genomic features, from clinical samples and investigating fine-scale taxonomy is a critical first step in investigating causality. Here, we describe the microbial diversity of samples associated with prostate cancer. Metagenomic assembly of non-human reads from the PanProstate Cancer Group, derived from blood, saliva samples and prostate tissue whole-genome data ( N = 247), successfully reconstructed 249 highly complete bacterial genomes, predominantly from oral samples. Our data, reveals eighteen bacterial species from the oral cavity without species level classification, while demonstrating a wide range of known species. This approach enables us to gain additional insights of the microbes in cancer patients at no additional sequencing cost and has the potential to reveal new links that could improve our understanding of cancer initiation and development.

title: Murine circadian disruption modulates gut microbiome and plasma metabolome dynamics in a sex- and age-dependent manner
abstract: Circadian disruption is a known driver of multisystem pathophysiology, yet how it interfaces with the gut microbiome and systemic metabolism across the life course, and how these interactions are shaped by biological sex, remains poorly defined. We performed longitudinal multi-omics characterization of Bmal1 -deficient mice in both sexes across three developmental stages. Ablation of Bmal1 induced core circadian disruption phenotypes, including reduced lifespan, decreased body weight, impaired glucose tolerance, and loss of locomotor rhythmicity, and drove sex- and age-dependent metabolic reprogramming, characterized by divergent insulin sensitivity and systemic lipid profiles. Loss of Bmal1 resulted in pronounced, sex- and age-dependent reorganization of gut microbial community structure and rhythmicity, with specific genera (e.g., norank_f_Muribaculaceae , norank_f_norank_o_Clostridia_UCG-014 , Bifidobacterium , Allobaculum ) exhibiting altered diurnal oscillations and divergent ecological trajectories across aging. Concurrent plasma metabolomic profiling unveiled sex‑specific metabolic variations and time‑of‑day‑dependent differences in circulating metabolites, suggesting coordinated disruption of microbiome-metabolome dynamics. Targeted quantification further revealed sex‑ and age‑specific alterations in plasma short‑chain fatty acids (SCFAs). Tissue‑specific gene expression analysis in the jejunum, colon, and liver revealed sexually dimorphic and age‑dependent transcriptional reprogramming of clock, barrier, inflammatory, and lipid‑metabolism genes, further underscoring the multi‑organ impact of Bmal1 deficiency. Integrated multi-omics correlation analysis demonstrated that associations between gut microbiome, plasma metabolites, and host glycolipid phenotypes are jointly shaped by sex and developmental age. Our findings identify aging and biological sex as pivotal, non-redundant ecological modifiers of circadian-associated host-microbiome interactions, underscoring the necessity of incorporating these variables into mechanistic models and translational strategies for circadian-related disorders.

title: C19orf18 modulates host susceptibility to Salmonella Typhimurium infection via remodeling of the gut microbiota and tryptophan metabolism
abstract: Chromosome 19 open reading frame 18 (C19orf18) is a protein-coding gene. On the basis of our preliminary findings, C19orf18 is selectively upregulated in the intestine of mice during Salmonella Typhimurium ( S . Tm) infection; however, its biological significance and functional role in the course of infection remain unclear. Here, we identify C19orf18 as a host factor associated with S . Tm-induced intestinal inflammation. Consistent results from both in vivo and in vitro experiments demonstrated that loss of C19orf18 function markedly attenuated S . Tm-induced intestinal inflammation and promoted mucosal injury repair. Mechanistically, C19orf18 deficiency was associated with the infection-associated gut ecosystem characterized by enrichment and expansion of Verrucomicrobiota, particularly the beneficial genus Akkermansia , and was associated with amino acid metabolic remodeling characterized by altered tryptophan-associated metabolic profiles. These tryptophan-associated metabolites were associated with epithelial restitution and suppression of inflammatory responses. Collectively, our findings reveal a previously unrecognized mechanism by which C19orf18 modulates host responses to a foodborne enteric pathogen and support a functional relationship among C19orf18-associated microbiota alterations, metabolic changes, and intestinal inflammatory outcomes.

title: Discovery of potent inhibitors of rumen methane metabolism via an AI-assisted workflow
abstract: Ruminant methane emission has attracted increasing attention due to its significance in global climate change and sustainable livestock production. Methyl-coenzyme M reductase (MCR), the key enzyme involved in the terminal step of methanogenesis in the rumen microbiome, is responsible for nearly all biologically generated methane released into the atmosphere. In this study, we developed an AI-assisted workflow for discovery of novel MCR inhibitors. Ultra-fast virtual screening of ~23 million molecules yielded 26 candidate molecules for experimental validation, among them 4 molecules showed significant inhibition of methane production. Subsequent structure-guided optimization led to the discovery of a nanomolar-range inhibitor P yra z ol-5(4H)- o ne,3-(4- n itrophenyl) (PZON) with an IC 50 of 0.24 μM. PZON inhibited Methanobrevibacter ruminantium M1 growth and methanogenesis in pure cultures, and suppressed methane emissions by 73–98% across rumen microbiomes from four ruminant sources, while exhibiting no detectable cytotoxicity at concentrations exceeding 400-fold its IC 50 . Metatranscriptomic analyses further demonstrated that PZON reduced transcriptional activity of diverse methanogenic lineages and MCR, providing transcriptional evidence of the anti-methanogenic activity of PZON. Overall, our study provides promising candidates for methane-reducing feed additives, and demonstrates the power of AI-assisted discovery of small molecules for targeted modulation of gastrointestinal microbiomes.

title: Guild-based microbial network links gut microbiota, serum metabolites, and bone mineral density
abstract: Although associations between the gut microbiota and bone mineral density (BMD) are increasingly recognized, existing evidence largely relies on taxonomic rather than ecological perspectives. How microbial communities function as integrated systems to influence BMD, and the role of serum metabolites, remain unclear. This study integrates gut metagenomic, serum metabolomic, and BMD data from 577 participants in the Taizhou Imaging Study. Employing a guild-based framework, we clustered gut microbiota into putative ecological units (guilds), identified BMD-associated guilds and serum metabolites, and explored mediating effects. Gut microbial diversity did not differ significantly among BMD groups, whereas co-occurrence networks showed different topological patterns: the osteoporotic network exhibited higher connectivity yet lower modularity, suggesting a less organized state. Guild-based analysis identified three candidate BMD-related guilds, and 15 serum metabolites, including amino acids and lipoprotein subfractions, were associated with BMD. Mediation analysis observed a statistical suppression effect in females, where very-low-density lipoprotein-1 triglycerides attenuated the observed positive correlation between a key guild (Guild_17) and its constituent species UBA11524_sp000437595 and BMD (Prop. mediated: − 25.48% and −30.39% at guild and species level). Our findings suggest that BMD is associated with altered gut microbial networks and lipoprotein profiles, providing observational evidence that may inform understanding of osteoporosis.

title: Complex interactions between Planctomycetota and their viruses in coastal marine sediments
abstract: Planctomycetota are widely distributed bacteria that play important roles in global element cycles, yet the diversity and ecological functions of their viruses remain poorly understood. Here, we recovered 326 Planctomycetota metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) and 96 associated viruses from coastal sediments of the Bohai Sea. These MAGs expand Planctomycetota diversity to 17 classes, including one novel class (currently assigned as class JAKEIC01 in GTDB Release 232) and 13 previously proposed classes. Most associated viruses belonged to Caudovirales , while 41 could not be assigned to known viral groups. Viral genomes encoded auxiliary metabolic genes involved in carbon and sulfur cycling. Analysis of host-virus interactions revealed diverse bacterial defense systems, including restriction-modification, abortive infection, and CRISPR-Cas. We identified three previously uncharacterized protein families associated with known phage resistance strategies, and their expression conferred antiviral resistance or enhanced neighboring defenses. Viral counter-defense strategies were also detected, indicating active host-virus interactions. Together, these findings provide new insights into Planctomycetota-virus interactions and bacterial immunity in marine sediments.

title: Large-scale multi-omics survey unveils microbial drivers of fermentation and flavor development across Mediterranean table olives
abstract: Table olives are a traditional fermented food typical of the Mediterranean countries. To become edible, they undergo diverse processes that shape their microbiome composition and flavor profile. By integrating shotgun metagenomics and volatilomics on 271 table olive samples from across the Mediterranean basin, we investigated how the technological process influences microbial communities and, in turn, the volatile organic compounds profiles. Indeed, naturally fermented olives showed enrichment of heterofermentative Lactic Acid Bacteria such as Lentilactobacillus buchneri , Lentilactobacillus rapi , and Pediococcus parvulus upon fermentation, that were highlighted as the main contributors to flavor development. We also highlighted the presence of bacteriophages targeting Lactiplantibacillus plantarum , providing novel insights into the modulatory role of the viral community, as well as the volatile organic compounds varietal fingerprints. This large‑scale multi‑omics investigation of table olives proposes new perspectives into microbial drivers of table olive quality, with potential implications for fermentation biocontrol and development of targeted starter cultures.

title: L-serine derived from the C-terminal region of Cry1Fa protoxin induces pathogenicity of an insect gut Enterococcus
abstract: The interactions between host, pathogen and gut microbiota can lead to outcomes in which the native bacteria can either enhance or attenuate the activity of the pathogen. Both have been reported for the microbiota of insects exposed to the Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) toxins. In this study, we identified a specific Enterococcus strain that becomes dominant in the gut of Spodoptera frugiperda following damage induced by Cry1Fa protoxin, and which accelerates host mortality. This dominance is accompanied by significant alterations in gut metabolite profiles, particularly amino acid levels, and we found that L-serine enhances the adaptability of the Enterococcus in the injured gut, increasing its abundance by up to 100-fold, and its translocation into the hemocoel. Moreover, supplementation with L-serine significantly increased Cry1Fa protoxin-induced mortality. Notably, the C-terminal region of the protoxin, previously reported to exert minimal direct insecticidal activity, serves as a source of L-serine upon proteolytic cleavage in the gut. Both L-serine and hydrolysate from the digested protoxin were found to encourage biofilm formation in the Enterococcus strain, providing a potential mechanism for its enhancement of protoxin activity. Our findings reveal a previously unrecognized function of the C-terminal of Cry protoxin, which suggests potential for the toxicity enhancement.

title: Clostridium butyricum attenuates subcutaneous fat deposition by remodeling intestinal extracellular vesicle-mediated gut-adipose communication in pigs
abstract: Whether intestinal extracellular vesicles (EVs) mediate the regulatory effect of C. butyricum on subcutaneous fat deposition remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated the effect of dietary C. butyricum supplementation on subcutaneous adiposity in Jinhua pigs and explored the potential involvement of colonic EVs in gut-adipose communication. C. butyricum reduced backfat thickness and adipocyte size, accompanied by lower expression of lipogenic and adipogenic genes. Furthermore, C. butyricum improved gut barrier function, reduced inflammatory markers, and increased microbial short-chain fatty acid production. Metagenomic analysis showed that CB-enriched microbial genomes harbored expanded carbohydrate-active enzyme repertoires, suggesting enhanced carbohydrate utilization and fermentation capacity. Intestinal EV profiling revealed that C. butyricum altered the abundance and miRNA cargo, which miR-1285 emerging as a functional candidate linked to adipocyte lipid metabolism. Integrated correlation and target analyses linked CB-responsive EV miRNAs with microbial functional guilds, pathways related to the regulation of adipogenesis and lipogenesis. Functionally, colonic EVs from CB-treated pigs and a miR-1285 mimic reduced lipid accumulation in adipocytes and suppressed lipogenic gene expression. These findings suggest that intestinal EVs may serve as a regulatory signal connecting C. butyricum -driven gut microbial remodeling to adipose lipid metabolic reprogramming.

title: Association between gut microbiome signature and blood pressure in children: findings from a Chinese cohort study
abstract: Childhood hypertension is a growing concern, yet its links with the gut microbiome remain poorly understood. We investigated prospective associations between gut microbial co-abundance groups (CAGs), dietary patterns, microbial metabolites, and hypertension risk among 1390 children from the Chinese Adolescent Cohort. Gut microbiota were clustered into CAGs, dietary patterns extracted via partial least squares regression, and associations with incident hypertension assessed using Cox models validated by elastic net regression. CAG1 (dominated by Faecalibacterium and Bacteroides ) and CAG5 ( Romboutsia and Blautia ) were associated with lower hypertension risk (HR = 0.56, 95% CI: 0.41–0.76; HR = 0.64, 95% CI: 0.45–0.91, respectively), whereas CAG3 ( Pseudomonas and Prevotella ) was associated with higher risk (HR = 1.40, 95% CI: 1.15–1.69). A CAG1-associated dietary pattern high in fiber, potassium, and vitamin A but low in sodium was protective. Fecal short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), including acetic acid (HR = 0.55) and propionic acid (HR = 0.28), were inversely associated with hypertension, mediating 69.6% and 41.4–68.8% of the CAG-hypertension associations, respectively, while CAG1 mediated 82.6% of the dietary pattern’s protective effect. Elastic net regression confirmed the microbiome-SCFA axis as a robust predictor, with acetic acid showing the strongest independent contribution. These findings highlight microbiome-targeted dietary strategies for early cardiovascular prevention.

title: A dispersal-recolonisation 3D biofilm in vitro model based on co-assembled peptide amphiphiles and clinical wound fluid
abstract: Chronic wound infections are sustained by dynamic three-dimensional (3D) biofilm cycles involving maturation, dispersal, and recolonisation, yet existing in vitro models fail to reproduce these temporal and structural complexities. Here, we report a strategy that co-assembles a designed protease-inhibitory peptide amphiphile (PA) with patient-derived wound fluid (WF) to reconstruct the complete biofilm life cycle in vitro. The PA sequence incorporates an HWGF motif capable of binding and inhibiting matrix metalloproteinase-9 (MMP-9), thereby preserving the integrity of recolonised biofilms under proteolytic stress. Co-assembling with WF generated a living material that mimicked the biochemical and mechanical microenvironment of chronic wounds, supporting the formation of stable 3D biofilms capable of dispersal and recolonisation. Furthermore, we established a controllable polymicrobial infection model and benchmarked its antibiotic-response trends against conventional susceptibility testing and in vivo spatial microbiological analyses. Notably, the antibiotic-response patterns of the PA/WF-derived biofilms closely mirrored those observed in a rat wound infection in vivo model. Collectively, our findings demonstrate that co-assembled living materials can recapitulate the nutritional composition, 3D architecture, and recolonisation dynamics of in vivo infectious biofilms, offering a physiologically relevant and customisable platform for investigating chronic wound infections and accelerating anti-biofilm drug discovery.

title: Living on the edge: survival strategies, biofilm, metabolites, and applications of aquatic extremophilic bacteria adaptation
abstract: Aquatic extremophilic bacteria from polar, deep-sea, and hypersaline environments reveal how life persists at physicochemical limits. Biofilm matrices act as dynamic interfaces that stabilize cells and organize metabolic cooperation, while specialized metabolites extend stress tolerance. Comparing these systems highlights a convergence on matrix-mediated strategies alongside environment-specific adaptations, positioning extremophilic biofilms as key models for microbial resilience and sources of novel biotechnological potential.
